title: The Replay
teaser: Someone just resigned. The project loses a month. The board meets in 15 minutes.
description: Jordan, the strongest contributor on Meridian's flagship project, has resigned to join another company, effective immediately. The project will be delayed by approximately one month. The player is the team lead, asked by the board to investigate before they convene in 15 minutes. All they have is an informal signal: a contact mentioned there may have been something more to Jordan's departure than the new role — nothing specific, no detail, just a sense that the official story might be incomplete. The board's question: 'What could have been done differently?' Three acts: (1) Diagnosis — scrub six weeks of project records, flag moments, build the chain of accumulating behaviours (credit misattribution, meeting moved, huddle exclusion, going quiet in week four). Workload flat throughout; what changed is reception, not volume. No single event is the reason. (2) Evidence — pick one moment, re-run with an intervention, watch the alternate branch. Early and small changes the trajectory; late and dramatic fails. The re-run answers the board's question with a demonstration, not rescue — Jordan has left and is not coming back. (3) Recommendation — assemble a board briefing: the chain, the re-run result, two free-text sentences (what happened, what should change), stored verbatim, never marked. A comfortable alternative ('Jordan received an attractive external offer; no further action') is available as a selectable option so the debrief can surface whether the team chose evidence or comfort. Red herrings: blunt feedback that was fair and acknowledged, a scheduling accident, Jordan snapping at a junior in week five, and a genuinely attractive external offer. Behavioural takeaway: people rarely leave over an incident; they leave over an accumulation nobody owned.
